title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure | WIRED
body:
# A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure

Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. [...] Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one [...] The researchers say that some of their crucial advancements are in developing a “human-AI collaboration process,” as Chaudhuri puts it, that allows agents to contribute and self-correct at almost every phase of the process while still seeking human input and review at key junctures. “We don’t want this sort of vibe world where AI is generating the goals and AI is generating the proofs and basically taking tests that are self-written," Chaudhuri says. “There’s a middle ground.”

Nvidia remains the leading AI infrastructure company, as its graphics processing units (GPUs) are still the primary chips used to power AI workloads. While Nvidia dominates much of the AI chip market, large hyperscalers are increasingly turning to custom AI accelerators to help reduce costs, especially when it comes to inference. title: Critical Red Hat Quay Flaw Lets Attackers Read and Overwrite All Private Container Images in a Registry
body:
Red Hat lists every version of Quay 3 and Quay 5 as affected by both flaws. For CVE-2026-123710, its guidance names standalone installs, Quay deployed by the Quay Operator on OpenShift, and the mirror registry for Red Hat OpenShift as affected.

Any Quay instance that untrusted clients can reach is exposed, including internal registries, the company says. [...] Cybersecurity

A second critical flaw, CVE-2026-110697 (CVSS score: 9.9), was disclosed at the same time. It lets a Quay user who can create a namespace steal other tenants' robot account tokens and use them to read, push, or overwrite those tenants' images.

This flaw is in the code that lists robot accounts. It builds an SQL LIKE pattern from the namespace name without escaping wildcard characters, and in SQL LIKE an underscore matches any single character. [...] Deleting the attacker's namespace also deletes the corresponding robot accounts, which can cut off systems that rely on them. Where Quay is the integrated registry for OpenShift, stolen robot credentials can be used to inject malicious images into CI/CD pipelines, the company says.

Red Hat's Dave O'Connor found both flaws. The logic behind CVE-2026-123710 has been in Quay since its first public commit, according to the bug report for that flaw.

title: This Actively Exploited Chrome Vulnerability Is Putting Your Browser at Risk | Lifehacker

That's bad enough on the surface, but, unfortunately, Google confirmed that CVE-2026-125350 has an active exploit in the wild. The company is keeping other details close to the vest, but it's dangerous nonetheless. At least someone, somewhere, has used this flaw against a target, which puts all Chrome users (as well as users of Chromium-based browsers) at risk.

What do you think so far? [...] As reported by The Hacker News, Google released a new update for Chrome on Monday that patches nine security flaws. While all vulnerabilities are important to patch, one in particular is more serious than the rest: CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component.

Lifehacker Logo

1. If you use Chrome, or a Chromium-based browser, your browser is vulnerable to an actively exploited security flaw.
2. CVE-2026-125350, a use-after-free flaw, allows for arbitrary code execution.
3. Google says it is aware that an exploit for this security flaw exists in the wild.
4. Chrome users can update their browsers today, but Chromium-based browsers will need to roll out their own updates.
